sentences.text: Byronosaurus was a small, graceful dinosaur belonging to the family Troodontidae, a group of maniraptorans closely related to birds.
This animal measured between 1.5 and 2 meters in length, stood 50 centimeters tall, and weighed anywhere from 4 to 20 kilograms.
Unlike most of its relatives, Byronosaurus lacked serrations on its teeth, a primitive trait it shares with the similar species Xixiasaurus.
It possessed a large brain relative to its body, forward-facing eye sockets for stereoscopic vision, and a nasal passage with windows similar to those found in birds.
Two skulls of this species have been found, with the largest measuring 23 centimeters, representing the best-known troodontids to date.
Researchers suggested that juvenile Byronosaurus skulls found in an oviraptorid nest were washed there from a nearby Byronosaurus nest by water flow.
The holotype, specimen IGM 100/983, was discovered in 1933 in the Djadochta Formation of the Gobi Desert, Mongolia, dating to the Late Campanian.
Mark Norell, Peter Makovicky, and James Clark formally named the type species Byronosaurus jaffei in 2000, honoring Byron Jaffe for his family's support of the expeditions.
Michael Novacek discovered the first skeleton in 1993 at Ukhaa Tolgod, followed by a second skull specimen found on July 15, 1996, at the Bolor's Hill site.
In 2009, two frontal skulls and lower jaws of very young individuals, perhaps recently hatched, were referred to Byronosaurus after originally being identified as Velociraptor specimens.
Troodontids, including Byronosaurus, possessed some of the highest encephalization quotients among non-avian dinosaurs.
Large eye-sockets and well-developed middle-ears suggest keen senses, while proportionately long legs indicate that these animals were agile.
Byronosaurus hunted insects and small vertebrates like lizards, fish, and mammals using needle-like teeth similar to those of primitive birds.
Mark Norell and colleagues described two juvenile specimens, neonates or embryos near hatching, found in an oviraptorosaur egg nest in the Late Cretaceous "Flaming Cliffs".
Byronosaurus is tentatively placed in the subfamily Troodontinae.
The species has been considered a member of the family Troodontidae since 2000.
Byronosaurus lived during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous, approximately 85 to 70 million years ago, specifically from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago, in what is now Asia.
In 2017, researchers suggested that juvenile specimens previously assigned to Byronosaurus actually belong to Almas ukhae due to differences in skull features like the number of maxillary teeth.

While Philip J. Currie and Dong Zhiming argued in 2001 that troodontids were carnivorous based on their serrated teeth, other researchers suggest the loss of serrations in Byronosaurus indicates a dietary shift to herbivory or omnivory.
Some researchers dispute the assignment of the juvenile skulls to Byronosaurus, and hypotheses for their presence in an oviraptorid nest include predation, scavenging by chicks, or brood parasitism.
